By Samuel L. Leiter

March 28, 2025. In 2023, two new musicals, Broadway’s How to Dance in Ohio and Off Broadway’s Buena Vista Social Club (at the Atlantic Theatre), were directly based on popular documentary films, each taking a different approach to mingling fact with fiction. The vastly superior latter was based on a 1999 Wim Wenders documentary. Its subject: a group of aging Havana musicians who, in 1996, created the eponymous, Grammy-winning, worldwide bestselling album of beloved Cuban songs. So affecting and musically absorbing was the show that my review begged for it to be brought uptown. The angels were listening because the show, even more gloriously, is now bringing Latin musical heaven to Broadway’s Gerald Schoenfeld Theatre. 

Historically, there were recording sessions like those in the show, of course, but just how much of the backstory was contrived is unclear, although the characters bear the names of the original performers. “Some of what follows is true,” we’re told early on, “Some of it only feels true.” The story is sufficiently convincing—unlike some of what transpired in How to Dance in Ohio—to provide a world and characters, a time and place, against which the thrillingly vibrant Afro-Cuban music comes to life. That assessment is as valid today as then, even with several significant cast changes.

The album’s premise is the reunion of a band of once-esteemed, mostly retired musicians whose careers withered during Fidel Castro’s regime, but who were rounded up by American Ry Cooder (who plays no part in the musical) and Cuban Juan de Marcos. In Marco Ramirez’s book, Juan (Justin Cunningham) is anxious to make an album of Cuba’s golden oldies using performers from when Batista was in power. They stayed behind instead of leaving Cuba when, in 1956, Fidel Castro’s revolution imperiled the venues—like the Buena Vista Social Club—at which bands like this performed.

Juan makes entreaties to the imperious diva Omara Portuondo (Natalie Venetia Belcon, magnificent as the iconic singer, 95 this year), a star who insists on doing everything her way. Having abandoned the spotlight for six years, she’s resistant, but Juan’s pitch gets her to eventually agree, thus bringing her back in touch with the men of her past. This sets up a structure that allows the show to toggle between 1996 and 1956. The leading roles are doubled to represent both the characters’ younger and older selves, which we sometimes see happen before our eyes. 

Fifteen songs, more than half from the original album, fill the theater with inexpressible joy and spirit, helping make the show as much a concert as a book musical. Ramirez’s slim but efficient book, however, is essential for contextualizing the performances, whose emotional impact would never have the same potency were the songs to lack connection with those who perform them. There’s just enough plot and character development to create sentimental value, historical background, and dramatic tension, creating a world in which a juke box musical can enthrall us for two hours of sheer joy. I was so taken by it Off Broadway that I looked forward to its Main Stem production more than to any other of this lively spring season; within minutes, this 84-year-old reviewer was dancing in his seat, clapping loudly, and shouting like a fan on “The Voice”!

As for its succinct dramatic content, there’s a central conflict between Young Omara (Isa Antonetti), who always wears a flower in her hair (like Billie Holiday) and her older sister Haydee (Ashlee De La Rosa). In 1956, the girls share an increasingly successful act performing for tourists at the upscale Tropicana Hotel. So good are they that Capitol Records wants to sign them to an American contract. When Cuba’s troubles heat up, Haydee insists they flee to the USA, but Omara, who wants only to “sing for our people,” can’t bring herself to leave. 

Partly that’s because of her relationship with a talented, dark-skinned performer, Ibrahim (1956: Wesley Wray; 1996: Mel Semé), who works as a busboy at the déclassé, non-discriminatory joint that gives the show its name. Racial issues in the music business, however, prevent the light-skinned Omara from continuing their budding partnership. (Casting can be problematic when skin color is involved; here, the older Omara is much darker than her younger version, but who cares!)

Arnulfo Maldonado’s marvelous three-walled set, with a large arch at either side, includes units that allow it to resemble a decaying old hotel lobby, a seedy night club, a recording studio, and so on. A cast of 18 is backed by a ten-member, always-present band. Saheem Ali’s inventive staging, David Yazbek’s creative consultation, Tyler Micoleau’s evocative lighting, and Dede Ayite’s impeccable costumes make you feel like you’re in Havana, even if you’ve never been there. 

Choreographers Patricia Delgado and Justin Peck, working with a compact, limber team of exuberant dancers, offer a cornucopia of Latin dancing, some of it balletic, much of it ballroom, all of it exciting, that will have you swaying in your seat, tapping your fingers, slapping your knees like bongos, dancing with someone in your head, and feeling your years and cares fall away. It’s almost impossible not to want to dance in place (which you can do a bit during the fully deserved standing ovation). 

Unless you know Spanish, you won’t understand the lyrics (there are no subtitles), but the expressive and rhythmic meaning of the music is never in doubt, ranging from sentimental to jubilant, with the accent on the latter. The songs aren’t there to contribute to the narrative or to reveal character. Being performed in a recording studio or nightclub setting, they’re simply to be enjoyed. A few you may instantly recognize, especially the upbeat conga number “El Cumbanchero,” a non-Cuban number made famous by Desi Arnez. You’ll love each one, whether it be “De Camino a la Vereda,” “Viente Años,” “Candela,” “El Cuarto de Tula,” or “Chan Chan,” to cite just a few at random. A very helpful little booklet is tucked into the program, giving the background to each number. 

You can’t escape their power to move you, whether sung by any of the marvelous singers—like Belcon, Antonetti, Semé, or Wray—or performed by remarkably virtuosic musicians—like tres player Eliades (Renesito Avich), woodwinds player Hery Paz, lightning-fingered pianist Rubén (1956: Leonardo Reyna; 1996: Jainardo Batista Sterling), or singer-guitarist Compay (1956: Da’von T. Moody; 1956: Julian Monge). In one predictable but nonetheless unforgettable moment, the haughty Omara refuses, when singing “Candela,” to allow flute music; when the musician (Hery Paz) joins in anyway, his trilling brilliance overcomes her resistance and melodic magic fills the stage.

The Broadway carousel is racing toward a sensational ending, with one promising show after another, especially the new (or extensively reconceived) musicals, grabbing for the golden rings of theatrical awards. Still ahead are such promising contenders as Boop: The Musical, Real Women Have Curves, Smash, Old Friends, Stranger Things, Floyd Collins, and Pirates: The Penzance Musical. Where Buena Vista Social Club will land when the carousel stops is anybody’s guess. I can say only that I haven’t seen a show this season whose music made me feel so euphoric. Can lightning strike twice? If music be the food of love, play on!

Buena Vista Social Club *****

By Paulanne Simmons

March 27, 2025. Sarah Snook‘s one-woman The Picture of Dorian Gray is a combination of melodrama and farce, enhanced by technology and enabled by sheer stamina. With the help of a team of camera operators and director and adapter Kip Williams, Snook relates the story of the unfortunate Gray both onscreen and off, playing a host of different people, some prerecorded, including the painter Basil Hallward; the hedonist Lord Henry Wotton;  the actress Sibyl Vane and her brother, James.

The show follows Oscar Wilde’s eponymous novel fairly faithfully: Basil Hallward paints a portrait of Dorian, and the handsome young man wishes the picture should age instead of him. After that it’s downhill for Dorian, who seduces Sibyl only to abandons her when he discovers she’s not a very good actress. After learning Sibyl has taken her life, Dorian vows to renounce love in favor of vice. James seeks revenge but ends up dead. It is the picture that executes the final retribution.

The staging surely is clever. The audience glimpses the camera operators taping Snook behind the screen as they watch her onscreen. We see her closeup, and closer up. We watch her interacting with her cell phone. Sometimes the video includes elaborate sets. Parts of the set appear onstage. We witness Snook changing costumes. The lighting and sound effects are dramatic.

But at the end of the play, what have we learned but the oft-repeated fact that Gray’s appearance remains youthful and innocent, while his portrait reflects the rot and age that have overtaken Gray’s soul? Wilde’s novel is more than a tale of Gothic horror. It is also a philosophical treatise. Wilde was concerned with the purpose of art and the value of beauty. He wanted the reader to think.

This production wants to frighten, entertain and impress. It’s the magician with one more trick. The showman saying, “You ain’t seen nothing yet.” Despite her versatility and dynamism, in the end Snook doesn’t so much play Gray as overwhelm him.

The Picture of Dorian Gray **

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

March 25, 2025. Two disparate musicals originating away from Broadway, one in London and the other Off-Broadway at the Atlantic Theatre Club, recently opened with a day of each other and separated by one theater. Operation Mincemeat debuted at the Golden and Buena Vista Social Club set up shop at the Schoenfeld (sandwiched between them is The Outsiders, last year’s Best Musical Tony winner, at the Jacobs.) Both shows take their inspiration from real events and spin dazzling entertainments out of them.

Operation Mincemeat is a riotously funny satire combining elements of Monty Python’s Flying Circus, Beyond the Fringe, and those marvelous movies depicting the British struggle to defeat Hitler such as The Battle of Britain, One of Our Aircraft Is Missing and The Imitation Game. A nimble cast of five (three of whom collaborated on the book, music and lyrics) play all the characters in a madcap send-up of stiff-upper-lip tributes to the English homefront and spy thrillers. The versatile ensemble crosses gender lines with ease with the three women playing numerous male roles and the two men enacting females with dexterity.

The truth-based plot follows the wacky scheme to deceive German intelligence by placing false information about British troop plans on the corpse of a derelict disguised as a pilot. Of course, there are twists and turns involving internal rivalries within MI5, Spanish coroners, Yank fliers, submarine crews and double agents. But along the way, we get innovative comedy numbers as well as believable character development. The participants in the stratagem are depicted not just as cartoonish caricatures but three-dimensional people with motivations beyond eliciting laughs. The clever script and score by David Cumming, Felix Hagan, Natasha Hodgson, and Zoe Roberts operates on several levels; it’s a musical spoof as well as a convincing espionage nail-biter. Robert Hastie’s fast-paced direction strikes the perfect balance between zany lampooning and honest portraiture.

The best example of this dichotomy of drama and comedy occurs when Jak Malone as Hester Leggatt, the ultra-efficient female staff member usually charged with preparing tea and taking dictation, makes a vital contribution to the operation. In the song “Dear Bill,” she creates a letter from a sweetheart to be placed on the cadaver to make his false mission convincing to the Germans. In Malone’s tender rendering, it becomes gradually clear that Hester is reliving a personal heartache from the previous war and the tragedy of combat and death intrudes on the breakneck farce. In contrast, Malone is delightfully ghoulish as the supplier of dead bodies and zestfully brash as an American pilot. In addition to “Dear Bill,” highlights include a shockingly funny Nazi number which approaches “Springtime for Hitler” from The Producers in its brash mockery and a Marx-Brothers mishmash involving hats and telephone chords as the status of the dead body is juggled between national authorities. Both of these and the rest of the zingy numbers feature Jenny Arnold’s inventive choreography.

Natasha Hodgson is appropriately pompous and narcissistic as the self-important, snobbish agent Ewen Montagu who steals the spotlight from Charles Cholmondeley (comically bashful David Cumming), a painfully introverted naturalist and the real creative genius behind the entire operation. Claire-Marie Hall sparkles as Jean Leslie, the secretary longing to emerge from behind the typewriter to make a real contribution to the war effort. Zoe Roberts bristles with authority as Johnny Bevan, the proper commander; zestfully parodies spy convention as Ian Fleming, the creator of James Bond; and is hilariously incompetent as a fumbling operative, Bond’s polar opposite. 

Ben Stones’ ingenious and flexible sets and costumes take us to dozens of locales from the Imperial War Rooms to muggy Spain to the skies over Europe in this madcap caper.

My only quibble is the cast tend to sing the clever lyrics to some of the patter-like numbers so quickly and in such proper British accents, it’s hard to comprehend all the words. But once you get used to the dialect and the rapidity, Operation Mincemeat is one of the funniest and most enjoyable shows of the past several seasons.

Two doors up at the Schoenfeld is another explosive entertainment, the Broadway transfer of Buena Vista Social Club. Based on the smash-hit 1997 album and Wim Wenders’ 1999 Oscar-nominated documentary, the musical focuses on the reassembling of musicians who frequented the titular informal establishment in pre-Castro Cuba. The book by Marco Ramirez supplies a mawkish storyline about retired diva Omara (a magnificent Natalie Venetia Beacon) reluctant to revisit her past, time-tripping between 1996 (the recording of the album) and 1956 (when the artists were beginning their careers before the revolution which shattered the country). But the real heartbeat of the show is the sizzling, energetic Afro-Cuban numbers, performed by the hottest ensemble on Broadway. The atmosphere is not as intimate as it was Off-Broadway, and the only changes are some elaborate, glitzy additions to Arnulfo Maldonado’s evocative set. Saheem Ali’s staging remains vibrant and fluid and the dancers are given more space to execute  Patricia Delgado and Justin Peck’s exciting, exquisite choreography.

In addition to Belcon’s commanding performance, Isa Antonetti, Julio Monge, Mel Seme, Ashley de la Rosa, and Wesley Wray turn in arresting work both dramatically and vocally. The real star is the galvanic ensemble, led by music director Marco Paguia who also is credited with orchestrations and arrangements. They and the cast make this the hottest party in town.

March 25, 2025. Two disparate musicals originating away from Broadway, one in London and the other Off-Broadway at the Atlantic Theatre Club, recently opened with a day of each other and separated by one theater. By Samuel L. Leiter

March 25, 2025. Despite its somewhat comedic title, Operation Mincemeat, the spectacularly clever British musical spoof (“spoofsical”?) at the John Golden Theatre, is inspired by an actual World War II deception operation of the same name. The successful ruse, concocted by two British Naval intelligence agents, Ewen Montagu and Charles Cholmondeley, involved the deployment of a homeless man’s corpse taken from a morgue—he had died from eating rat poison—to be dressed as the faux Royal Marines Major Bill Martin with false documents on him. The dead man’s real name was Glyndwr Michael, and he’s honored in the show and in the Playbill. 

When the supposedly drowned body was discovered off the Spanish coast, it deceived the Germans into believing that the Allies were planning to invade Greece and Sardinia, not Sicily as was expected. This this led the Germans to shift their troops from Sicily, leaving it ripe for a nearly bloodless Allied invasion. 

This is the outline for a true story filled with surprising twists and turns (including developments about the discovery and disposition of the corpse), which the show exploits for comic mayhem with remarkable adroitness. Amazingly, as this detailed plot summary reveals, it takes a few liberties but nevertheless sticks close enough to the historical events; noticeably, it leaves Greece out of the equation. But it does connect, to deliciously amusing effect, the very real relationship of all this to Ian Fleming and his master spy creation, James Bond.

Well before this new show—which arrives here after a multi-award-winning London run—was conceived, its fascinating core of wartime espionage was exploited in various media. These include a 1950 novel by a former cabinet minister; The Man Who Never Was, a 1953 nonfiction best seller by Ewen Montagu himself; a similarly titled 1956 movie of that book, starring Clifton Webb, Gloria Grahame, and Stephen Boyd (here’s the trailer); Montagu’s 1977 autobiography, which filled in more background; a 2010 book by Ben Macintyre; television dramas; the 2022 movie Operation Mincemeat, with Colin Firth and Matthew Macfadyen; and several earlier, 21st-century plays and musicals. Operation Mincemeat, although not as well known on these shores as across the pond, is obviously a gift that keeps on giving.

It would seem that most of the story’s previous retellings have leaned heavily on its serious, even melodramatic qualities—obviously present in its two film versions—but to see in it material for a broadly comic musical took a stroke of genius. Lively, ingeniously inventive, and sometimes raucously hysterical, the show’s many characters are played by five gloriously versatile actors, three crossing the gender line, and all based on those working for MI5. These posh-accented ladies and gents are agents Montagu (Natasha Hodgson) and Cholmondeley (David Cumming), Colonel Johnny Bevan (Zoë Roberts), and proto-feminists Jean Leslie (Claire-Marie Hall), a clerk, and Hester Leggatt (Jak Malone), a secretary and administrator. Of course, everyone plays other characters, usually accompanied by split-second costume changes.

Operation Mincemeat, born in 2019,is the maiden production of a group called SplitLip, founded in 2017. Amazingly, its creators knew little about musical theatre when they took it on, thus allowing them to break the rules without knowing what the rules were. The idea was hatched when, on vacation with her family in Norway, Hodgson’s brother had her listen to a podcast about the operation, and she realized the story’s potential as a musical. 

Its book, lyrics, and music are the offspring of Hodgson, musician Felix Hagan, and two others of its company, Cumming and Roberts. They may not have known much about musical theatre but they all have talent at singing and theatrical physicality, especially when it comes to musical clowning. Directed with unimaginable imagination by Robert Hastie and choreographed with hilarious brio by Jenny Arnold, it doesn’t stand or sit still for two and a half hours; its excessive length is perhaps its principle flaw. There’s just so much cyclonic farcing an audience can take before its attention span and physical needs begin vying for attention.

Operation Mincemeat is performed, for the most part, in an odd, supposedly underground room (designed by Ben Stone, who also did the smashing period costumes) with walls of black tile, phones on the distressed walls, and a rear wall that allows for all kinds of unique, often geometric lighting effects (by Mark Henderson). It has something of a music hall revue quality, the actors occasionally acknowledging the audience while clearly having a grand old time carrying on as if they were in a cartoonish Monty Python-like sketch. 

The songs, many sung in rat-a-tat-tat fashion, have patter-type lyrics, piling rhythmic rhymes on rhythmic rhymes, although, musically, no matter how amusing, a few sound, at first hearing, like others. Each song, though, holds surprises, if you’re able to catch the rapidly spewed lyrics first time around, which isn’t always an easy task. And, with The Producers’ “Springtime for Hitler” having demonstrated that most audiences will get the joke, Act Two opens with five Nazis doing a K-Pop-style boys’ band number, “Das Übermensch,” with lyrics like these: 

NAZI 4: This is the Reich on the mic, the Übermensch in ya brains 

Adding adrenaline to the Aryan blood in your veins 

NAZI 1: With our fascism fashion, yo we’ve got style for days 

And you know 

ALL: Deutschland Uber Alles is our favourite phrase!

When the house bursts into loud applause for this Nazi bunch, Col. Bevan appears, looks at us with disdain, and asks, “Really?,” sparking one of the show’s biggest laughs.

The standout number for me, though, is the sentimental “Dear Bill,” which comes as close to a conventional ballad as the show allows. Sung by Hester, and based on her recollections of her own World War I romance, it’s meant as an example of how to write a letter to one’s lover off at war, listing the mundane things of daily life the lover is missing. The lines “And why did we meet in the middle of a war? What a silly thing for anyone to do?” are threaded through it. I clapped as hard as anybody, especially as it was touchingly, and straightforwardly, rendered by Jak Malone, who won an Olivier Award on the West End. Malone plays a woman here, expressed by little more than a black curl sitting on his brow, but also does a memorable turn as a macho, broadly American pilot. I’m betting there’s a Tony nom in this guy’s immediate future.

In fact, I’ll be surprised if, even in this season of Broadway musical theater, in which new straight plays are disappointingly rare, the Operation Mincemeat itself doesn’t pick up a slew of nominations and awards. There may be some heavier hitters out there, but wouldn’t it be fun if this little show were to make mincemeat of them?

Operation Mincemeat *****
The Golden Theatre, 252 W 45th St., NYC. 
Running time: 2 hours, 35 mins. with 20 mins. intermission. operationbroadway.com
Through August 18, 2025.

By Paulanne Simmons

March 23, 2025. Satires on war are perhaps as old as war itself. Consider Lysistrata, M*A*S*H, Catch-22 and now, Operation Mincemeat, the very energetic and occasionally funny West End import by David Cumming, Felix Hagan, Natasha Hodgson and Zoë Roberts. It turns out, however, that Operation Mincemeat is based on a true story. In fact, that story has already been made into a film starring Colin Firth, also called Operation Mincemeat. And the film was based on  a book by The Times columnist Ben Macintyre.

It’s not a bad idea to review any of the source material before seeing this musical, as the British accents and the poor sound at The Golden Theatre make it sometimes difficult to figure out what’s going on. But by the second act, it should become clear that a group of British agents, desperate to stop the German war machine, adopts the nerdy Charlie Cholmondeley’s plan to convince the German’s that Great Britain is about to invade Sardinia instead of Sicily. 

But, of course, the devil is in the details. The idea is to find an unidentified corpse, dress it up in a British military uniform, provide it with the necessary papers and take it by submarine to the coast of neutral Spain. The hope is that the corpse and the papers will be discovered, and the papers will make their way to Hitler, who will be properly misinformed.

Operation Piecemeal is performed by an ensemble of five actors (Cumming, Claire-Marie Hall, Hodgson, Jak Malone and Roberts) directed by Robert Hastie. The humor is based not only on the ridiculous situation but also the equally ridiculous characters, many of whom are played by cross-dressing actors. Charlie is an amateur naturalist obsessed with newts. Ewan Montagu (Hodgson) is an incompetent braggart. Hestor Leggatt is a stolid middle-aged secretary whom the brilliant Jak Malone makes both comical and moving.

In fact, the best song in the show is Hester’s “Dear Bill,” in which she pens a fake love letter, which turns into a very real love letter to her own lover who was killed in World War I. Other songs that work well are the peppy and sarcastic “Born to Lead” and the stirring “Sail On, Boys.”

The show’s humor is very British and very self-referential. At numerous times, the audience is  slyly reminded they are watching a musical. There’s also a good deal of slapstick. One scene with telephones and hats is reminiscent of the Marx Brothers.

Ben Stones has given the show a single unit set which encloses the action nicely, while allowing for various props to emerge from the wings and the fly space. This is indeed a colorful show.

Operation Mincemeat takes too long to get going and too long to end. But in between there are some very enjoyable moments.

Operation Mincemeat ***

By Samuel L. Leiter

March 22, 2025. Family dramas are theatrical staples, especially the kind where relatives gather from far and wide for some unifying function, like a holiday, death, or birthday. Often, a contentious dinner forms a central scene, as in August: Osage County (2007) or this season’s Cult of Love. In Tony-winning Branden Jacobs-Jenkin’s Purpose, now at the Helen Hayes Theater, such a scene, at a belated birthday party, perfectly captures the dynamic of a disparate family group (catalyzed by an outsider’s presence) so worked up they barely have time to snatch a bite.

And there’s plenty to be worked up about in Purpose, originated (like August: Osage County), at Chicago’s great Steppenwolf Theater last year, and, as with the playwright’s Pulitzer Prize-winning last play, Appropriate (about a white family facing racist issues), worthy of another. In it, he takes two hours and 50 minutes to dissect the Jaspers, iconic elites in African American circles, not terribly unlike the Jesse Jackson family. 

The Jackson avatar is the self-satisfied pater familias Solomon “Sonny” Jasper (Harry Lennix, commanding and resonant), a renowned politician, civil rights leader, and itinerant preacher. He and his magisterial—sometime lawyer—wife, Claudine (LaTanya Richardson Jackson, a force of nature), manage the family legacy, trying to keep their clay feet from crumbling as a landslide of secrets, lies, and bad choices threatens to engulf them.

Setting the tone for director Phylicia Rashad’s fiercely impressive production is Todd Rosenthal’s imposing set for the Jasper’s Chicago manse, a towering living room with an upstairs landing leading via a winding staircase to the spacious living room below. A dining area, with a large round table, sits up right before a big window through which snow continues to fall. Portraits of significant Black leaders—dominated by one of Martin Luther King, Jr.—share space with other artifacts of Black culture. Amith Chandrashaker creates the perfect lighting, and Dede Ayite the character-defining costumes.

Solomon’s younger son, Nazareth, dubbed Naz (Jon Michael Hall, outstanding), who narrates and explains the events, dropped out of divinity school to become a nature photographer. Although he identifies as “asexual,” he’s donated his sperm to Aziza Houston (Kara Young, spirited), a deed meant to remain their personal secret. Such news, fears Naz, would surely blast Solomon and Claudine’s moral standards to smithereens.

Aziza, a queer Harlem friend with a degree in social work and a strong interest in civil rights, has driven him here from Niagara Falls, and is heading back home. Persuaded to sleep over by the overpowering Claudine, who imagines a romantic relationship between the visitor and her son, she’s overwhelmed to discover that Naz’s parents are the Jaspers, whom she holds in the highest esteem. She soon, however, finds out not only more about them than she would have preferred to know. 

Meanwhile, she meets Solomon’s energetic but unstable son, Junior (Glenn Davis, excellent), a state senator, just released from 30 months in prison (like Jesse Jackson, Jr.) for misusing campaign funds. His angry wife, Morgan (Alana Arenas, ferocious), is disturbed because, now that Junior’s been released, she has to serve a year herself for a related white-collar crime. Their children have been left by her at home, away from their grandparents’ influence. 

As the evening wears on, the dysfunctional relationships among the Jaspers come into sharp focus in multiple subplots, introducing talk of sexuality, religiosity, incarceration, heritage, adultery, mental illness, beekeeping (!), and, as forcibly articulated by Solomon before the final curtain, the need for purpose in one’s life. It’s hard not to see hints of Williams’s Cat on a Hot Tin Roof peeping through, and even of Chekhov. 

The first act plays swiftly and with great gobs of comedic panache mingled with dollops of serious concerns. Jacobs-Jenkins’s gift for rhetorical fireworks are on full display, especially when projected by the booming voice of the charismatic Solomon Jasper, whose voluble attacks on the pathetic Junior are painful to behold.

Act Two focuses less on the ensemble than one-on-one or two-on-one confrontations, with perhaps a tad too much time spent on monologues that practically become disquisitions and can sometimes sound more practiced than spontaneous. The tone is darker, which, ironically, serves to heighten the relatively fewer laugh lines, which receive eruptions when they come, because they contrast so sharply with their harsh surroundings. Wait, for example, for the house-rocking questions Solomon can’t resist asking Naz about his experience as a sperm donor. 

The only thing that might have prevented Purpose from keeping my eyes and ears glued to the stage throughout its nearly three hours was the incredibly cramped conditions of my seat in Row N. I’ve never felt quite so compressed at the Hayes, so I wonder if some rows have even less elbow and knee room than others. (I’m forced to concur with the Chicago reviewer who called Purpose “a work of knee-buckling intensity.”) And, of course, such a long show in a theater with such a limited restroom creates an interminable bathroom line, which, for the first time ever, forced me to miss the opening of Act Two as I waited with others to be let back in.

Broadway is booming with new musicals this season, but new straight plays have been few and far between. And not much more is promised for April, when the season ends. As such, Purpose will be on every best play list. But even in a season with more competition, it would dominate. You won’t want to miss it; just leave your knees at home.

Purpose ****1/2
Helen Hayes Theater, 240 W. 44th Street, NYC
Running time: 2 hours and 50 minutes, including one 15 minute intermission. www.purposeonbroadway.com
Through July 6, 2025.
Photography: Marc J. Franklin

By David Sheward

March 22, 2025. “There is no straight line to tell this story,” says Joshua, the character standing in for the playwright Joshua Harmon in his touching autobiographical work We Had a World on the smaller stage of Manhattan Theater Club’s City Center Off-Broadway space. As the author-narrator says, the narrative of Joshua and his fraught relationship with his grandmother Renee and mother Ellen zig-zags chronologically across three decades, telling and retelling family events from a trio of different perspectives. 

The play is savagely funny and heartbreakingly savage in its compassionate depiction of dysfunction and devotion, skillfully directed by Trip Cullman and acted with depth and tenderness by a dazzling cast of three—charming and chipper Andrew Barth Feldman as the stand-in for the author, endearing and maddening Joanna Gleason as the grandmother, and in a brilliant turn, versatile Jeanine Serralles who manages to make us empathize with the manipulative mother. 

We begin with a phone conversation between Renee and her grandson Joshua, informing him she has his next play all ready for him. It will be called Battle of the Titans. It will take place in her apartment during Rosh Hashanah when Renee has invited both of her daughters—Joshua’s mother Ellen and Ellen’s estranged sister Susan. “It will be Virginia Woolf, Part II,” Renee promises. We are also informed that 94-year-old Renee has been diagnosed with cancer and this will probably be her last family gathering. From this launching point, Joshua tells us the complicated, love-hate story of his relationships with his mom and grandma. (Susan’s gripe with Ellen is never fully developed in one of the few weaknesses of the script.) At first, Renee comes across as a delightful Auntie Mame-type, treating the pre-teen Joshua to such sophisticated, mature artistic fare as Robert Mapplethorpe photo exhibits, the Broadway revival of The Heiress starring Cherry Jones, and mature movies such Secrets and Lies and Dances With Wolves.

But Ellen interrupts the action, demanding to tell her side of the story. We gradually learn the fun-loving Renee was also a chronic alcoholic. Going further back into past, Ellen paints a frightening picture of her childhood, far different from Joshua’s idyllic recollections of his. Harmon masterfully portrays the varying perspectives of his characters, giving each equal weight and creating a triple-barreled view of the same events. One perfectly-written example details the acquisition of two antique loveseats during a family trip to France, home of the trio’s ancestors (Sidenote: Harmon takes on the French branch of the clan in his Drama Desk Award-winning Prayer for the French Republic.) Renee, Ellen and Joshua convey their versions of the loveseat story as well as their disparate attitudes towards the furniture (Renee and Joshua love them, Ellen hates them.) World careens through recollections with the three actors occasionally playing other roles, staged fluidly by Cullman so that the vignettes flow into each other like streams feeding into a river of memory. 

Feldman makes a sturdy narrator, guiding us through the labyrinthine paths of Harmon family history and colorfully registering ambiguous reactions to the two most important women in Joshua’s life. Gleason is effervescent and bubbly in conveying Renee’s sparkling charm, but she also reveals the toxicity in this woman’s brand of champagne. Serralles offers the most complex and detailed performance as the resentful Ellen. Self-described as “a bitch who gets things done,” Ellen takes on the burden of guilt and responsibility while caring for her alcoholic mother. Seralles artfully conveys Ellen’s ambiguous feelings towards her mom and son through telling details and gestures. Watch as she carefully and precisely folds the wrapping paper of two unwanted gifts from Josh, then shoves the presents under the hated loveseat. Whether impatiently shaking a foot, piling pots and pans with rage, or just letting a crooked smile creep across her otherwise frozen face, Seralles lets us know what Ellen is feeling or thinking about her impossible, but beloved family. It’s a memorable performance in one of the top family plays of recent years.

John Lee Beatty’s suggestive set creates the atmosphere of a rehearsal of a work-in-progress, lit with attention to mood by Ben Stanton.

We Had A World ****
Manhattan Theater Club at NY City Center Stage II, 131 W. 55th St., NYC.
Running time: One hour and 50 mins with no intermission. nycitycenter.org

content.rendered:
By David Sheward

March 20, 2025. Sex plays a vital role in three classics works, now in revival Off-Broadway: Tennessee Williams’ A Streetcar Named Desire, Henrik Ibsen’s Ghosts and, surprisingly, Anton Chekhov’s Uncle Vanya in a solo adaptation called simply Vanya. How the directors and casts handle this hot topic determines the success or faltering of each show. 

Williams’ Streetcar has had a total of nine Broadway productions since its debut in 1947 as well as numerous film and TV incarnations. But few have matched, let alone eclipsed, the impact made by Marlon Brando as the brutal, charismatic Stanley Kowalski in the original and immortalized in Elia Kazan’s 1951 film adaptation which also elevated Vivien Leigh’s delicate, shattered Blanche DuBois to icon status. (Sadly all that remains of Jessica Tandy’s Broadway original is a recording of one scene. Her praised performance lives on only in memory and written reviews.) Rebecca Frecknall’s innovative Almeida Theater staging, now at BAM’s Harvey Theater after Olivier Award-winning engagements in London, has divided critics. But I found it perfectly captured Williams’ elemental battle between the primitive Stanley and the delusional Blanche.

I was not as enthusiastic about Frecknall’s assault-and-battery approach to Cabaret which is still running on Broadway at the August Wilson. But her imaginative minimalist interpretation is more effective here. Stripped of scenery and accompanied by a deafening percussive score (composed by Angus MacRae and performed vigorously by Tom Penn), Williams’ immortal play becomes a combat ballet like Stravinsky’s Rite of Spring. Figures from Blanche’s imagination such as her dead, gay husband (Jabez Sykes) and the messenger-of-death flower seller (Gabriela Garcia) insert themselves into the action in expressive dance movements. 

Film and TV hunk Paul Mescal is a commanding Stanley, holding his own against memories of Brando. He prowls and runs around set designer Madeleine Girling’s raised platform like a tiger, ready to pounce. But the production is dominated by Patsy Ferran’s jittery, chatty Blanche. Barely holding herself together, her Blanche is teetering on the edge of hysteria at every moment, desperately staving off madness with alcohol, cigarettes, and flirtation. The sexual connection between her and Stanley is percolating beneath their every interaction, making his molestation of her inevitable. 

Anjana Vasan’s solid Stella (Stanley’s wife and Blanche’s sister) grounds the production and understudy Eduardo Ackerman (subbing for Dwane Walcott at the performance attended) delivered an embattled Mitch, torn between his attraction for Blanche and his revulsion at her promiscuous past. This Streetcar has primal force behind it but the new, uneven Ghosts does not.

When Ibsen’s Ghosts was first published in 1881 and staged a year later, it caused a scandal, not just because it frankly dealt with the corrosive effects of venereal disease, but also because it took an unflinching look at how the repression of the natural sexual urge can destroy lives. So it’s unfortunate that Jack O’Brien’s otherwise proficient production of the play in a decent new translation by Irish playwright Mark O’Rowe at Lincoln Center’s Mitzi Newhouse Theater is drained of carnal energy. 

Written not long after Ibsen had espoused pre-feminist themes in A Doll’s House, Ghosts also exposes the hypocrisies and destructiveness in conventional, “respectable” society. The main character is Mrs. Alving (a powerful Lily Rabe), a widow about to open an orphanage as a memorial to her supposedly noble late husband. In fact, Alving was an alcoholic libertine whose sterling reputation was a facade created by his industrious wife. She is now paying the price for her spouse’s sexual excesses. Her beloved son Oswald (a lackluster Levon Hawke) has inherited syphilis and his health is deteriorating to the point of incapacity. (Remember, this was before a shot of penicillin could fix you up.) 

Ibsen’s main thesis is that sexual repression leads to the ruination of all the characters. Mrs. Alving explains that her spouse became a drunken reprobate because of the puritanical mores of Norwegian society. Despite some strong liming and direction, the production fails because there is no animal chemistry between the actors. There is no spark igniting between Oswald and the maid Regina (a feisty Ella Beatty) who turns out to be the illegitimate daughter of Alving and therefore Oswald’s half-sister (introducing yet another taboo topic: incest). There is a similar lack of fire flicking between Mrs. Alving and Pastor Manders (Billy Crudup, appropriately buttoned-up) whose long-ago mutual attraction was smothered by their overweening sense of moral duty. In Richard Eyre’s memorable production which played BAM in 2015, there was a considerable passionate connection between Lesley Manville and Will Keen in those roles.

In addition, O’Brien unnecessarily brackets the action with a contemporary conceit. Before the action starts, sound designers Scott Lehrer and Mark Bennett bombard the audience with a cacophony of contemporary street noise—including car horns. When the lights dim, the actors inaudibly repeat the first few lines of the play while reading scripts. Hamish Linklater as Engstrand, Regina’s nominal father, tapes a wooden block to his foot to simulate his character’s bum leg. At the play’s finish, the cast angrily flings their scripts on set designer John Lee Beatty’s elegant long table. What’s the purpose of this alienation effect? To remind us we’re watching a play? That the dominant repressive attitudes espoused by the larger culture of Ibsen’s time are still prevalent today? These ideas should be clear without calling attention to themselves.  

Despite these flaws, there is a dynamic energy here, particularly when Lily Rabe is debating her unfortunate life choices with the self-righteous Manders. You can see her indignation rising and her attempts to keep it down as she is accused of espousing non-conventional mores. When she counters Manders’ arguments in favor of stifling sensuality, her unique voice, a blend of razor blades and honey, quivers with barely suppressed anger. Rabe conveys Mrs. Alving’s conflicted passions as she wrestles with the consequences of her husband’s prolificacy and her cover-up. Crudup has a raw force as Manders, but, as noted, the physical urge is not there and makes him a less equal partner to Rabe. Hawke (the son of Ethan Hawke and Uma Thurman) as Oswald lacks the necessary fire to ignite his role. Beatty (the daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Benning) does display a comic flair with Regina’s attempts to appear sophisticated as she shows off her elementary French. She also rises to the occasion of outrage when Regina learns the truth of her parentage and exits Mrs. Alving’s house, slamming the door like Nora in A Doll’s House. Linklater imbues Engstrand with an intense desperation as he tries to reclaim his daughter and his identity. 

John Lee Beatty’s set, lit with meaning shadows by Japhy Weideman, creates the appropriate Gothic atmosphere, but without a fleshly element, this Ghosts fails to haunt.

While this revival of Ghosts lacks sexual heat, Andrew Scott’s solo adaptation of Chekhov’s Uncle Vanya, just called Vanya, now at the Lortel Theatre Off-Broadway after a smash London run, positively reeks of it. Adapted and co-created by Simon Stephens, (director Sam Yates is also credited as co-creator), this one-man version of the classic depiction of blighted, frustrated lives on a Russian country estate contains not only the usually-overlooked carnal component, but also a galaxy of emotions beautifully delineated characterizations by Scott in a tour de force performance. 

Unlike the clumsy brief modern interpolations in O’Brien’s Ghosts, Stephens’ updating is unobtrusive, plus his contemporary dialogue feels natural and appropriate to the characters. Though the pompous professor Alexander is now a filmmaker and Scott gives the characters a variety of dialects ranging from posh British to country Irish, Chekhov’s Russian tale of unrealized dreams has never felt more intimate and relevant. Scott endows each of the eight characters with a distinct personality, aided with a simple prop for each. 

Rather than the usual melancholy brooder, Scott’s Vanya is a manic comic, cavorting around Rosanna Vize’s contemporary set which resembles a combination industrial break room and a rehearsal studio. (Vize is also a co-creator.) This Vanya masks his depression with a manic court-jester vitality. He announces every entrance or mood swing with a sound-effects gizmo issuing canned laughter or popping in a music cassette. Michael, the dissipated doctor, conveys his nervous energy by bouncing a tennis ball. Vanya’s unhappy niece Sonia, pining with unrequited love for Michael, folds and refolds a red handkerchief to express her longing.   

Scott and his collaborators even give life to Anna, Vanya’s late sister and Alexander’s first wife. This character is not on stage, but her spirit is symbolized by the family piano evocatively playing itself at the appropriate moments. 

In addition to convincingly differentiated between the roles, Scott delivers a plethora of moods, passions and subtextual memories. He is unafraid of silence, allowing the slightest whispered line conveying concealed passion to resonate and reverberate in quiet moments. He’s also unafraid of sex, unflinchingly acting out the lust between Michael and Helena, Alexander’s second, much younger wife. As in Streetcar, but not Ghosts, the physical element is definitely felt in Vanya. 

A Streetcar Named Desire ****

By Samuel L. Leiter

March 19, 2025. We Had a World, the new, three-character, autobiographical dramedy by Joshua Harmon, Off Broadway at Manhattan Theatre Club’s City Center Stage II, is like the play many of us have in our heads when we think about how we might put our own family stories into writing. We may even think that the next time the family gets together, we’ll record the conversations, transfer them to the page, and make a play out of them. In fact, such a transcript is enacted late in We Had a World, which concerns Joshua, a gay, Jewish playwright growing up under the influence of a grandmother, Renee, and mother, Ellen, who never stop bickering, often because of grandma’s drinking.

Harmon, of course, is a professional playwright (mentioned in the play) with a strong track record (Skintight, Bad Jews, Prayer for the French Republic) with the skills most of us lack to shape his memories into a framework that holds our interest for an hour and a half. His material and characters are not unfamiliar (apart, perhaps, from the alcoholic Jewish grandma), but his dialogue—infused with snarkily comic throwaways—has the ring of authenticity, the acting is mostly effective, and Trip Cullman’s directing keeps everything humming.

Renee (a.k.a. Nana), played with just the right amount of eccentricity by the wonderful Joanna Gleason, wearing a shoulder-length gray wig, is a kind of Auntie Mame to the fascinated Joshua (Andrew Barth Feldman, effectively transitioning from early childhood to maturity and in between). The boy loves escaping from his suburban home to visit her at her tastefully decorated Upper East Side apartment, sparingly reflected in John Lee Beatty’s set, nicely lit by Ben Stanton, a more-or-less open space on a wooden platform, allowing for multiple locales. 

Notable are a carved, wooden loveseat and a chair, representing, but in no way replicating the two high-backed loveseats prominently mentioned in the play. Kaye Voyce’s costumes are otherwise appropriate, but the idea of having young Joshua seen at the opening in nothing but his jockey shorts as he takes a phone call from Nana is both ridiculous and exploitative.

Harmon pours into the blender his memories of Ellen and Nana over the years from 1988, when he was around five, to 2018, when Renee, at 93, was fatally stricken with pancreatic cancer. The mixture is a nonlinear play that moves freely—and sometimes hazily—back and forth in time, as Joshua narrates the events while also living through them. Renee and Ellen also get to narrate bits and pieces, so the acting requires rapid emotional transitions from scene to scene, going from dialogue to direct address, often in the voice of other (unseen characters). You must listen closely, as it’s easy to get confused, especially when only the context reveals when there’s a time and place shift. 

Harmon’s premise is that the ailing Renee asked him to write a play about the family called Battle of the Titans, and to make it “as bitter and vitriolic as possible.” She hoped it would be Virginia Woolf: Part II.  It does reach that toxic goal here and there, but it’s also infused with warm affection for the boy’s beloved grandma, a flashy Hungarian immigrant who nonetheless affects a posh British accent. She introduces grade school-aged Joshua to avantgarde exhibitions of X-rated artists like Robert Mapplethorpe, a Broadway revival of Medea, and R-rated movies like Dances with Wolves. Her quirky proclivities include badgering museum personnel with questions. In return, Joshua teaches Nana things she finds useful, like saving water by turning the faucet off when brushing your teeth.

Ellen, a busy attorney, is played by a fiery Jeanine Serralles with chip-on-her-shoulder bitterness (which she sometimes overdoes). She bears a deep-seated grudge against her sister, Susan, for a reason that seems trivial but, within the painful dynamics that alienate so many family members from one another, is perfectly plausible. (I speak from experience.) So harsh can such feelings be that siblings will not only speak to one another but refuse to be in the same room. Ellen lashes out at Renee for her boozy lapses (like when she walked out of a school show in which Joshua appeared), or for inviting Susan to a family seder. Still, despite saying her mother “is not a good person,” she does manage to maintain her daughterly responsibilities when Renee goes on hospice care.

The play tosses bits and piece of the past into the blender, summer camp in Switzerland, a family book club, the above-mentioned loveseats Nana bought in Paris in 1960, Joshua’s internship with Miramax (run by Harvey Weinstein!), therapy, study in France, a lost backpack in Italy, and so on. The characters talk about relative Jewish piety, Joshua’s coming out, a secret about Renee’s past, parental responsibilities, Joshua’s boyfriend, dealing with imminent death, and so on, the discourse sometimes enhanced by revelatory letters Joshua discovers. There’s even room for political jabs, like Renee’s, “The great United States is at the mercy of this idiot.”

All this, and more, adds up to, not so much a conventional play, but a catalogue of tiffs and disagreements, anecdotes and recollections that remind us of our own families, and, perhaps asks us to contemplate our own mothers, and the role they played in our lives. But be reminded, We Had a World is not I Remember Mama.

We Had a World ***

title.rendered: Five Reasons Why Redwood Reaches Soaring Heights

content.rendered:
By Iris Wiener

March 19, 2025. Tony-Award winner Idina Menzel (Wicked) sure knows how to make a much-anticipated return to Broadway. She currently stars in Redwood, a musical that she co-conceived with director, book writer, and co-lyricist Tina Landau. Menzel plays Jesse, an art gallery owner who finds herself at a crossroads as she grieves the loss of her son. She leaves her wife (De’Adre Aziza) and life behind as she drives cross country in an effort to come to terms with her new existence. Her self-discovery and psyche evolve and heal as she spends several days on a Northern California redwood tree. Though the new musical features many ballads by newcomer Kate Diaz that tend to blend together in a forgettable whole, the production’s design is stellar in and of itself. Here are just some of the reasons why Redwood soars:

1. The true star of this show is within the title itself. The sensational design of Redwood’s tree is realistic in a profound way; it leaves one feeling as though they are one with nature, imagining every groove, crevice, and brittle section of the bark as Menzel and her co-stars scale it. In fact, it is so lifelike that Jesse names it Stella. The characters explore many metaphors for growth with the backdrop of the redwood (look for the song “Roots”), but none of them are more inspiring than the beauty of scenic designer Jason Ardizzone-West’s tree.

2. Projections and video are often used in theatres of all shapes and sizes these days, but none to a more gripping effect than those in Redwood. With screens extending to all pockets of the house, wrapping around the boxes and soaring into the mezzanine, the show often feels as encompassing as one in a planetarium. When coupled with Hana S. Kim’s video design, it envelopes audiences in serenity, truly transporting them outside of their Manhattan realm.

3. Scott Zielinski’s lighting design and Jonathan Deans’ sound are masterful, especially in an intensely climactic moment involving a massive fire. The resonance of the sensitive material in the aftermath of the Los Angeles fires is only heightened with the energy and storytelling provided by the expert lighting and sound. Redwood features flashbacks and hallucinatory moments that are as emotional as they are jarring, but easily palpable due to the design of the transitions provided by these elements. 

4. Jesse runs into two botanists, Finn (Michael Park) and Becca (Khaila Wilcoxon), who are visiting the great redwood with the purpose of surveying it. Both Park and Wilcoxon immediately connect with audiences: Park, through his humor and tender, relatable relationship with Finn’s son, and Wilcoxon as she comes to terms with Jesse’s need to seemingly infringe on Finn and Becca’s work. Look for powerful numbers “Little Redwood” and “Becca’s Song,” which reveal as much about the tree as they do about her moving motivations for a career in conserving nature.  

5. Idina’s vocal gifts are aptly showcased here, with long, high notes that soar in sadly unremarkable songs. For theatre mavens, Redwood holds a meaningful layer of nostalgia, as it marks Idina’s return to the Nederlander Theatre where she made her Broadway debut in Rent 29 years ago. Audiences will appreciate Jesse’s emotional journey throughout Redwood as much as they will celebrate Menzel’s growth in her full-circle moment. One can’t help but hear the ghost of Rent’s Maureen in the leaves of this Redwood, whispering with pride.

Running time: 85 mins. with no intermission. cur8.com

By Paulanne Simmons

March 17, 2025. If you’re a fan of country music, and especially the music of songwriter JT Harding, you’ll definitely like Bedlam’s Music City. The show is directed by Eric Tucker and features a talented cast of musicians, who play various instruments while they sing many of the songs from Harding’s catalogue.

The main conceit of  the show is that the audience is sitting in a Nashville dive bar called the Wicked Tickle, watching performers at an open mic. Scenic designer Clifton Chadick has set up a bunch of tables facing a grubby stage, with a bar not too far off. And the audience sees not only what happens onstage but also behind the scenes: drug deals, music industry machinations, familial problems, romance.

The main problem with the show is Peter Zinn’s book, which is too long, too complicated, too predictable and too unbelievable. 

It goes like this: Two songwriting brothers, TJ (Stephen Michael Spencer) and Drew (Jonathan Judge-Russo), are trying to get their big break in Nashville when they meet a mysterious singer named 23 (Casey Shuler), and TJ falls for her like a ton of bricks. Things look good for a while, especially when Nashville agent Leanne (Leenya Rideout) hears them singing their party anthem “Y’allsome” and is so impressed she decides they’d be the perfect songwriters for her client, the famous country singer Stucky Stiles (Andrew Rothenberg). 

However, as the musical unfolds, many problems impede the romance and the brothers’ career. Here they are: Stiles, who is also impressed with what he hears at the Wicked Tickle, attempts to lure 23 away from TJ by recording a hit song with her. But even worse, TJ has figured out the best way to get the funds he needs to launch his career is by selling drugs for a lisping lout named Bakerman, also played by Rothenberg, whose exaggerated portrayal of evil would make even a child laugh. And one of TJ’s clients is none other than 23’s mother, Tammy, also played by Rideout, who sometimes seems to confuse her two parts. The doubling up of actors does not help the complicated plot.

Finally, in a bizarre twist, TJ joins the National Guard and is sent overseas when several U.S. embassies are attacked. But if you haven’t guessed by now, he survives and returns just in time to win the lady and sing one more song.

Intermittently the show is interrupted by country dancing choreographed by John Heginbotham. Neither the choreography nor the dancers seem sufficiently accomplished to warrant the interruption of either the messy plot or the robust music.

As its name might imply, Bedlam prides itself on its mission to “invigorate traditional forms in a flexible, raw space.” In other words, they want to shake things up. A noble enterprise. But sometimes it just creates… well… bedlam.

Music City ***
West End Theatre, 263 West 86th Street, NYC. 
Running time: 135 mins.
Closed March 2, 2025 after extending twice.
Photography: Daniel Rader

By Samuel L. Leiter

March 15, 2025. Norwegian playwright Henrik Ibsen’s Ghosts, now in an uninspired production at Lincoln Center’s Mitzi E. Newhouse Theatre, has not received anywhere near the number of New York revivals as A Doll’s House, the slightly earlier Ibsen play considered its opposite face. In the latter, first staged in 1879, a young woman, finding herself in an untenable marriage, walks out on her family, a choice that shocked conventional morality. In Ghosts, published in 1881 but not professionally performed for nearly a decade, a middle-aged widow, who left her debauched husband after only a year of marriage, compromised her principles and returned to his side, setting the stage for tragedy.

The play’s confrontation with 19th-century conservatism, which includes a character dying of venereal disease, attacks on religious faith, and, among other things, a potentially incestuous liaison, also led to ferocious protests, from liberals as well as conservatives.

For the current version, Mark O’Rowe has condensed the three-act play into a single, 95-minute act, directed by the venerable Jack O’Brien, with four of its five-member cast—as Marvin Carlson would argue in his book The Haunted Stage—eliciting ghosts of their theatrical parents. Lily Rabe (daughter of actor Jill Clayburgh and playwright David Rabe) is Helena Alving, widow of the late Capt. Alving, a lecherous drunk; Levon Hawke (son of actors Ethan Hawke and Una Thurman) is Oswald, Mrs. Alving’s son, a painter newly home from Paris, suffering from a venereal disease (syphilis most likely); Ella Beatty (daughter of actors Annette Bening and Warren Beatty) is Regina, social-climbing maid fathered by Capt. Alving with another woman but believing the carpenter Engstrand to be her father; and Hamish Linklater (son of Kristin Linklater, renowned actors’ vocal coach), is the alcoholic Engstrand, hoping to open a home for sailors where Regina can work. The only non-nepo baby is Billy Crudup as Pastor Manders, the uptight cleric who believes a wife must do her wifely duties no matter how repulsive her husband is.

O’Rowe’s abbreviated version of Ghosts is to be welcomed, given that the play has seen its day; without either a brilliant concept or an exceptional cast, a full-length version might have proved excruciating. As it is, it suffers from occasional longueurs, including the overextended, lachrymose denouement, when Oswald, after explaining his illness to Mrs. Alving, collapses and loses his mind as he continues to babble for the sun.

The play’s implausibility alarm buzzes now and then, most loudly when the otherwise defiantly progressive Mrs. Alving allows Pastor Manders, who fears censure for not trusting God to preserve it, to talk her into not insuring the new orphanage she’s about to christen. The foreshadowing is so dense, as Manders keeps pestering her, that you know the minute Mrs. Alving agrees what the result will be. I suspect that compressing the play also tends to highlight its melodramatics, which stand out that much more sharply with fewer words to say.

Ghosts was once explosively important, a drama that moved the modern theatre’s needle further into territory commensurate with society’s advances. It seems today more like an artifact, interesting as a reflection of a moment in theatre history, its value more educational than artistic. Even the great Jack O’Brien has been unable to shape from it anything more than a passable event. He starts the play, inexplicably, by having the actors appear as themselves, reading from handheld scripts, before they put the books aside and enter the play. Now and then, he moves the action forward, almost as if editing a movie, by shifting the lighting (creatively designed by Japhy Weidman) with a bump, accompanied by a subtle sound (designed by Scott Lerner and Mark Bennett).

O’Brien works on a barely decorated set designed by the inimitable John Lee Beatty: large, windowed panels upstage looking out onto persistent rain; a square wooden platform; a massive wooden table; chandeliers. And not much else. Jess Goldstein’s black and white costumes are problematic: they suggest an indeterminate time, softly hinting at the late 19th century for some, being practically contemporary for others. Regina’s black dress barely covers her knees, for example, while Mrs. Alving’s is floor length but not the pile of fabric and bustles a woman would have worn in the 1880s. And Oswald wears an odd white getup that could easily be pajamas or some artfully fashionable item he picked up while living in Paris. Perhaps clothing closer to the play’s period might have helped make its moral dilemmas more pertinent.

The cast is led by Lily Rabe, who, at 42, is a bit more youthful than most Mrs. Alvings; her vocal, physical, and intellectual qualities allow her to give the most qualified performance. Billy Crudup, his good looks hidden under a gray beard, is out-of-place as Pastor Manders, his energetic outbursts, both playful and angry, seeming almost compensatory for a lack of gravitas. And whatever subtextual romantic feelings exist between Manders and Mrs. Alving rarely surface. Levon Hawke’s flaccid Oswald needs much more dimension and texture, while Ella Beatty’s flirtatious Regina, with her too perfectly coiffed long hair, seems more Feydeau than Ibsen. Last and, I’m afraid, least, Hamish Linklater’s Engstrand looks and acts like the ragpicker of Paris.

Ghosts, given its reputation in the canon, will continue to be revived, of course. It will need better productions than this one, though, if it isn’t going to give up the ghost.

GHOSTS **1/2

By: David Sheward

March 10, 2025. At first Lisa Sanaye Dring’s Sumo, at the Public Theater in a co-production with Ma-Yi Theater Company and La Jolla Playhouse, seems to be plotted like so many familiar sports movies. The scrappy underdeveloped kid struggles manfully to build himself up and fulfill his dream of making it to the top. The grizzled veteran treats him harshly to toughen him up for the impossible climb. Commercial interests distract the newcomer, but he eventually triumphs on the athletic field. 

Dring’s script does contain these cliched tropes, but she also incorporates deep character development and a complex meditation on the sport of sumo itself and its relation to Japan’s cultural heritage. Director Ralph B. Pena and fight directors James Yaegashi and Chelsea Pace create muscular and fast-moving staging for both the scenes related to the story and the fascinating sumo matches to which the all-male cast commits themselves fully. Taiko drummer Shih-Wei Wu provides dynamic percussive accompaniment. Hana S. Kim’s spectacular, gorgeous video designs, Paul Whitaker’s scene-shifting lighting, and Wilson Chin’s sumo-ring setting create a varied and intense arena for ideas and conflicting ambitions.

Narrating the action and offering commentary are three Shinto priests or Kannushi (Paco Tolson, Kris Bona, and Viet Vo in drily comic turns.) We follow the young protagonist Akio (Scott Keiji Takeda in an impressive Off-Broadway debut) as he progresses from lowly apprentice to champion. The borderline sadistic grand master Mitsuo (a commanding David Shih) drives Akio hard, even resorting to physical abuse. Along the way, Dring gives us a crash course in the significance of sumo and its religious, mythological origins. The rigid ceremony of massive mammoths pushing each other until one is on the ground or outside the ring is much more than grunting and sweating. Dring explores the mystical meaning of the ceremonies to its participants and spectators. She also charts the interrelationships and delicate emotions of the members of Mitsuo’s heya or stable. 

In addition to Akio, there are Ren and Fumio (compelling Ahad Kamal and Red Concepcion) whose clandestine romantic union provides a moving subplot, the earnest So (tender Michael Hisamoto), and Shinta (funny and heartbreaking Earl T. Kim) whose bulk belies his sympathetic nature. Gradually the majority of the wrestlers’ human flaws force them to drop out of the heya, leaving only Akio and Mitsuo. Ultimately, Akio must chose between the rigid macho strictures of Mitsuo and a more empathetic approach to his beloved sport. Dring’s plot arc is a bit predictable, but her thoughtful examination of sumo culture and Pena’s exhilarating staging make this a gripping takedown match.

SUMO ***1/2

title.rendered: THE GREAT PRIVATION (HOW TO FLIP TEN CENTS INTO A DOLLAR) ***

content.rendered:
By: Samuel L. Leiter

March 10, 2025. It’s good to see the always daring Soho Rep back in business, with Nia Akilah Robinson’s The Great Privation (How to flip ten cents into a dollar), after having to give up its funky storefront space downtown on Walker Street. The company, devoted to innovative experimental work, is now comfortably ensconced (for the next few years, we’re told) in the 99-seat Peter Jay Sharp Theatre, on the fourth floor at Playwrights Horizons. While I wasn’t enamored of the play (first staged at London’s Theatre503 last year), whose biblically allusive title I still don’t get, its acting, direction, and design elements maintain the Rep’s high standards.

The Great Privation reflects our compulsion to understand ourselves as products of our families’ historic backgrounds, especially where traumatic events have occurred. Here, it’s an African American family, with the intent of emphasizing how buried Black bodies, lacking agency,  were not allowed to remain at rest, but were disinterred for scientific purposes meant, according to the script, to benefit only whites. The compulsion to dig into our pasts, painful or not, is universal, as represented by success of Ancestry.com and similar outlets for our curiosity.

In the case of The Great Privation, it’s an African American family represented by a mother and her daughter, as viewed in time-contrasting sequences that go back and forth between 1832 and today. In the past, the mother, in her 30s, and her 16-year-old daughter (Crystal Lucas-Perry and Clarissa Vickerie) are Missy and Charity Freeman; in the modern scenes they’re Minnie and Charity Chillous. 

On designer Marian Sánchez’s mostly bare stage, atmospherically lighted by Marika Kent, we see an earth-colored floor of what resemble large ceramic tiles; on them stands a gnarly old tree whose thick surface seems a gathering of twisting, limb-like accretions, perhaps meant to suggest the many souls buried there. In 1832, this is the graveyard of Philadelphia’s African Baptist Church; today it’s a campground for white kids. The same four actors appear in both periods; the connection between the historical and contemporary characters is too slim to view the latter as avatars of the former, but a hint of it nevertheless hovers. Kara Harmon’s effective costumes help make the time differences work. 

Missy and Charity are first observed in the wee hours of the morning guarding the grave of their just- buried husband/father, Moses, a victim of the city’s cholera epidemic. Students from a nearby medical college have been robbing the graves of fresh victims to study them in the interests of understanding the disease. The grave robber we meet, a white man named John Petersburg (Miles G. Jackson), says Moses’s body must be exhumed within three days if it’s going to have any scientific value. 

Perhaps this explains the digital clock overhead whose red numerals count down to zero from 72:00:00, regardless of it being the past or present, until stopping three-quarters of the way through the play. Whatever its purpose, it comes off as the kind of head-scratching distraction with which experimental dramatists like to tinker. 

We also meet the medical school’s Black janitor (the one-named Holiday), who explains the business arrangements behind the purchase of Moses’s body, whose exhumation Missy tries to prevent by claiming his soul needs the time to travel back to its homeland in Sierra Leone.

In the present-day scenes, set at the campground, John is a campy camp counselor. The actor who played the janitor is Cuffee, the camp’s first-ever Black supervisor, who happens to be a former sex partner of John’s, whatever dramatic value that is meant to provide. Loose connections between John and the events of 1832 are made, Moses’s skull plays a big part (a Hamlet reference sneaks its way in), surrealistic episodes intrude, and the 95-minute, intermissionless play finally is laid to rest.

Evren Odcikin’s smart staging offers much to appreciate, but, mostly, Robinson’s play works on a moment-to-moment basis. She supplies comedy (some funny, some not), lively dance sequences, and even a finale using a fourth wall-breaking, clap-along, musical number. However, the episodic play has too many such distractions, rarely comes into sharp focus or clarifies its purpose, and, much of the time, provides little what-happens-next tension. Considering that The Great Privation’s themes have been labeled “profound,” I was surprised to find their expression so frequently commonplace.

Holding it all together is its sterling cast. Crystal Lucas-Perry (Ain’t No Mo) is a dynamo of fortitude and wit as Missy/Minnie. Clarissa Vickerie, soon-to-graduate from Julliard with an MFA, is making her Off-Broadway debut as Charity (although looking anything but 16); her ability to mine comic nuances vividly through facial and kinetic expression makes her contribution invaluable. By David Sheward

March 7, 2025. Just as August Wilson centered most of his dramas of the African-American experience in his home city of Pittsburgh, Samuel D. Hunter has returned again and again to his native state of Idaho to chronicle the damaged lives of its residents and those who have left, but still nurse their hurts received there. Hunter has focused on the fraught relationships between queer and straight Idahoans in affecting dramas like Pocatello, The Whale, A Case for the Existence of God (winner of the New York Drama Critics Circle Award), and his latest, perhaps most searing play, Grangeville now at Signature Theater. 

We begin in total darkness, listening to the disembodied phone voices of two estranged half-brothers Jerry and Arnold (Paul Sparks and Brian J.Smith in riveting, heart-wrenching performances). As the conversation progresses and the lights gradually dim up, we learn that Jerry and Arnold have different fathers but the same mother who is in failing health (spot-on sound by Christopher Darbassie and lighting by Stacey Derosier). Truck driver Jerry has been caring for their mom in the titular town in Idaho, while artist Arnold is living in Rotterdam with his husband, a museum curator, and has not been in contact with the family for years. Jerry needs help dealing with Mom’s disorganized medical bills, but he also wants to re-establish relations with the younger Arnold. The attempts at reweaving the frayed bond between the half-siblings forms the thread of the play and Hunter sensitively explores the nature of family trauma and the need for forgiveness and coping with suffering.

Though Sparks and Smith are the only two actors, they also play each other’s partners in separate scenes. In what could have come across as a gimmick, the performers and director Jack Serio manage to make this difficult double casting work. Smith subtly plays Jerry’s ex-wife Tracy without descending into female caricature and Sparks takes on Arnold’s spouse, the Dutch Brom with surprising delicacy. But it is in their portraits of the two brothers that the pair are most shattering. Sparks compassionately limns Jerry’s guilt over physically abusing Arnold when they were kids and his earnest desire to make amends. He’s also particularly funny when Jerry tries to wraps his working-class mind around artistic concepts. Neither the playwright or the actor are condescending here. Smith taps into Arnold’s rage at the ill-treatment he received as a young gay man in a homophobic society and builds a careful scaffolding of icy reserve around this damaged soul. When that edifice comes crashing down and the siblings finally reach out to other figuratively and literally, it’s devastating.

In addition to the double-casting aspect, Sergio takes on the tricky task of the characters having to play scenes via cell phones and Zoom meetings. Jerry and Arnold only occupy the same actual space in the final scene. But Sergio conquers this obstacle by having the actors relate to each other as if there were in physical proximity throughout. His understated direction and the spare set by the dots design team perfectly captures the blistering emotions evoked in Hunter’s tender two-hander.

By Samuel L. Leiter

March 4, 2025. Raviv Joseph, whose plays, like Bengal Tiger at the Baghdad Gates (a 2010 Pulitzer finalist), Guards at the Taj, and King James, have made him one of the most admired American playwrights of the past two decades, has not added greatly to his laurels with his latest effort. A two-hander called Dakar 2000, it’s being shown in a Manhattan Theatre Club production flatly directed by May Adrales at City Center Stage I, starring newcomer Abubakr Ali (the film Anything’s Possible)and veteran Mia Barron (The Wolves).

In a role apparently based to some degree on Joseph’s own experiences as a Peace Corps volunteer in Kaolak, Senegal, West Africa, in the late 1990s, Ali plays the 25-year-old Boubacar (nickname: Boubs), who shares not only Joseph’s job description but the playwright’s half-Indian, half-white ethnicity. The play proper is set at the very end of 1999—just as the world is holding its breath about the potential damage of Y2K—but Boubs, speaking at the end of 2024, narrates the opening and closing monologues looking no different than a quarter century earlier. 

In the first monologue, where he tells us he sometimes serves as an espionage courier, he suggests that not everything he says or that we’ll hear in the play can be trusted to be the truth. We then witness a series of gotcha moments in which the truth is constantly being toyed with by its two characters, as they engage in cat and mouse confabulations.  

This isn’t a time travel tale, however, but what, inexplicably, some viewers have called a “thriller.” Yes, it has a spy story premise, and Boubs, asked to serve as a field agent for the State Department, carries out a dangerous assignment that makes him feel like James Bond, wanting even more such work. Nevertheless, the potential for thrills is dissipated by talky ruminations, dull pacing, and lackluster acting.

The official who recruits Boubs is Dina (Barron), an attractive woman in her mid-40s, who puts him on the spot after requisitioning materials for himself that he instead donated to a group of women building a garden and well. When she threatens him with deportation home, Ali, with no meaning in his life outside of his Peace Corps work, sees such an outcome as a fate worse than death, and becomes a sucker for Dina’s goals.

Dina has been searching for the man behind the bombing of the US embassy in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania in 1998, an actual incident that she claims killed her close friends, whose deaths she’s desperate to avenge. (If, indeed, that’s true.) The suspect happens to be at her hotel on New Year’s Eve, the night Boubs thought he was going to score with Dina. (He boasts that he’s brought 30 condoms!) Boubs must sneak into his room, dressed as a bellhop, and fingerprint him as he lies asleep, knocked out by a sedative, if he is, indeed, still alive. Or did Boubs unwittingly kill the guy with a poisoned fingerprint pad? Regardless of its promise, the brief scene in which he carries out his mission in the darkened room barely manages to stir a tingle.

Boubs is a naïve do-gooder, whose innocence the crafty Dina—who has studied interrogation methods—easily manipulates for her own purposes, even using the promise of sex as an inducement. The idea of a bedroom dalliance between these chemically mismatched characters is about as plausible as thinking Trump, Zelinsky, and Vance would turn to the cameras after their recent White House blowup, smile, and say, “Live from D.C., it’s Saturday night!”

Ali plays Boubs as such a boob that it’s impossible to take him seriously, or to engage with the situation in a way that fosters mental and emotional involvement. For all the actor’s histrionic tricks, very few moments in his overacted performance bear any resemblance to a real human being. Barron brings to Dina—a role you can imagine being played by someone like Elizabeth Marvel or Allison Janney—little beyond stereotypical line readings and behavior.  

On top of this, Joseph introduces various diversions, such as hifalutin speculation and thoughts on things like Y2K, fate, the Hale Bopp comet, and wondering if our existence is only a simulation. There is also a dramatically flaccid, boringly romantic rooftop scene under a starlit sky, and a dramaturgic inability to wrap things up without overdoing the blather. Whatever thrills Dakar 2000 may have promised have been smothered in a blanket of overwriting.

Adrales’s staging uses a revolving set by Tim Macabee, with a sweeping comma-shaped ramp, that allows for the several locations to easily move off and on. Much as it seems guilty of overkill for this intimate show, it benefits from effective lighting by Alan C. Edwards, appropriate costuming (Boubs wears localized items, including a wool cap) by Emily Rebholz, and projections by Shawn Duan (starlit skies are wearing out their welcome). 

Dakar 2000, which has received a wide mix of critical reactions, a good number more positive than mine, will likely be widely produced because of its writer’s reputation, small cast, and relatively low budget needs. Here’s hoping some at least put the thrill back into it.
